name: Lisbon
description: Hilly coastal capital with tiled streets, custard tarts, fado music and easy day trips to Sintra and the beach.
languages: English (widely spoken in Lisbon, Porto, and Algarve)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Contactless card payments are standard, but carry small cash in Euros for historic trams (like Tram 28), small pastelarias (custard tart shops), and taxis.

culturalTips: Appetizers brought to your table (bread, olives, cheese) are NOT free; you only pay if you eat them, or you can politely decline them.
Tipping is not standard: leaving 5-10% in sit-down restaurants for good service is appreciated, but large American tips are not expected.
Dinner starts around 8:00 PM or later; arriving at 6:00 PM will find empty restaurants.
Portuguese are proud of their distinct identity: never speak Spanish assuming it is interchangeable with Portuguese.

languages: English (widely spoken in Lisbon, Porto, and Algarve)

name: Barcelona
description: Gaudi architecture, tapas bars and city beaches. Watch for pickpockets in crowded areas.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Contactless card and phone payments are universal for almost all amounts. Keep €10-20 cash for small rural bars, churro stalls, or public restrooms.

culturalTips: Daily schedule is shifted 2-3 hours later than in the U.S.: lunch is 1:30-3:30 PM, and dinner is rarely before 8:30 or 9:00 PM.
Tipping: Leaving 5-10% in sit-down restaurants or leaving small change at tapas bars is generous; American-style 20% tips are not expected.
Watch out for pickpocketing in crowded areas (especially Barcelona's Las Ramblas, metro, and busy plazas).
Tapas are traditionally social finger foods eaten standing up at the bar counter with a small beer ('caña') or wine.

name: Paris
description: Museums, cafes, bakeries and iconic landmarks, best explored on foot.
languages: English (widely understood in Paris and major tourist hubs)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Nearly cashless. Contactless cards and Apple Pay work in almost all boulangeries and cafes for even a €1.30 croissant.

culturalTips: Always say 'Bonjour' (or 'Bonsoir') immediately upon entering any shop or cafe before saying anything else; omitting this is considered rude.
The bill already includes a 15% service charge by law ('service compris'); leaving an extra €1-3 in cash for good service is customary.
Dining is an unhurried social ritual; waitstaff will not bring the bill until you explicitly ask for it ('L'addition, s'il vous plaît').
Speak at a lower volume in restaurants and metro trains compared to typical U.S. outdoor voices.

name: Rome
description: Ancient ruins, Renaissance churches and classic pasta, with history on nearly every block.
languages: English (understood in major tourist centers, less so in countryside)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Contactless card payments are widely accepted, but small cash in Euros is useful for espresso at coffee bars, gelato, and city hotel tourist taxes ('tassa di soggiorno').

culturalTips: Coffee etiquette: Cappuccino and milky coffees are considered breakfast drinks—ordering a cappuccino after 11:00 AM or with a heavy meal looks strange to locals (order an 'espresso' or 'caffè' instead).
The 'coperto' on restaurant bills is a legal bread and cover charge per person; American-style 20% tips are not expected (leaving €1-2 in coins is generous).
Strict dress codes apply in Catholic basilicas (St. Peter's, Duomo): shoulders and knees MUST be covered for both men and women.
Validate train and bus tickets in yellow/green stamping machines before boarding to avoid steep on-the-spot fines.

languages: English (understood in major tourist centers, less so in countryside)

name: London
description: Free major museums, markets, theater and pubs across a huge variety of neighborhoods.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Virtually 100% cashless. Contactless cards and phones are used everywhere, including London buses, Tube gates, street performers, and pubs.

culturalTips: In traditional pubs, there is no table service: order food and drinks directly at the bar counter and pay on the spot.
Always stand on the RIGHT on London Underground escalators to allow people to walk on the left.
Queuing is a deeply ingrained cultural value; never cut in line.
A 12.5% discretionary service charge is frequently added to restaurant bills; check your receipt before tipping additionally.

name: Edinburgh
description: Medieval old town, a castle on a volcanic rock and easy access to Highland day trips.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Virtually 100% cashless. Contactless cards and phones are used everywhere, including London buses, Tube gates, street performers, and pubs.

culturalTips: In traditional pubs, there is no table service: order food and drinks directly at the bar counter and pay on the spot.

name: Dublin
description: Pubs with live music, literary history and quick trips to coastal cliffs.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Nearly cashless. Contactless cards and smartphones are accepted everywhere from rural pubs to city buses.

culturalTips: In pubs, buying drinks operates on the 'round system': if someone buys you a pint, you are expected to buy the next round when your group is ready.
Tipping: 10-12% in sit-down restaurants with table service is standard; tipping bartenders at pub counters is not customary.
Friendly banter ('the craic') and storytelling are central to Irish social life.
Always thank the bus driver when stepping off public buses ('Thanks!').

name: Amsterdam
description: Canals, bike-friendly streets and major museums.
languages: English (fluently spoken by ~95% of the population)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Heavily cashless country ('PIN only'). Many Dutch supermarkets (like Albert Heijn) and cafes do NOT accept cash at all.

culturalTips: Tipping: Service is included; rounding up to the nearest euro or leaving 5-10% for good dinner service is customary, but large tips are not expected.
Watch out for bike paths (red asphalt painted with bike symbols)—cyclists have right of way and will ring bells loudly if you step into their lane.
Direct communication: Dutch people are famously egalitarian, candid, and direct; do not interpret straightforwardness as rudeness.
'Coffeeshops' sell cannabis; regular cafes that serve coffee and pastries are called 'Koffiehuis' or 'Café'.

name: Copenhagen
description: Design-forward city with great food, harbor swimming in summer and bikes everywhere.
languages: English (fluently spoken by nearly 90% of the population)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Practically 100% cashless. Cash is actively discouraged in many cafes, bars, and public transport systems.

culturalTips: Tipping is NOT customary; service charges, fair living wages, and high taxes are all included in menu prices.
Respect dedicated bicycle lanes—never stand or walk in bike lanes, as cyclists commute at high speeds and have the right of way.
'Hygge' (coziness and contentment) values warm candlelight, relaxed conversation, and informal social warmth.
Punctuality is essential for both social and business appointments.

name: Berlin
description: Cold War history, street art, museums and famously late nightlife.
languages: English (widely spoken, especially among younger Germans & in cities)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash is culturally favored. Many bakeries, beer gardens, kiosks (Spätis), and small restaurants are strictly CASH ONLY ('Nur Bares'). Keep €30-50 in cash on you.

culturalTips: Tipping: Tell the server the total amount including a 5-10% tip when handing over cash or card ('Stimmt so' means keep the change).
Do NOT jaywalk when the pedestrian light is red, especially in front of children—locals will openly call you out.
Bottled beers and sodas have a refundable deposit ('Pfand'); return the empty bottle to the supermarket reverse vending machine for your coins back.
Direct, candid communication is normal and considered respectful honesty, not rudeness.

name: Prague
description: Fairy-tale old town, castle views and inexpensive beer and food.
languages: English (widely spoken in Prague and tourist spots)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Card acceptance is very high in Prague, but traditional pubs ('hospoda') and smaller towns still prefer or require cash.

culturalTips: In pubs, servers will keep bringing fresh beers as soon as your glass is empty until you place a beer coaster on top of your glass.
Tipping in restaurants: Round up or add 10% directly when the bill is presented; do not leave coins on the table.
Always remove your shoes when entering a Czech private home.
Avoid changing money at street kiosks in Prague with zero-commission signs (often massive hidden margins); use bank ATMs instead.

name: Vienna
description: Imperial palaces, classical music, coffee houses and Christmas markets.

cardsLimited: American Express (accepted mainly in luxury venues)
paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash is strongly preferred in traditional coffeehouses, Heuriger taverns, and bakeries. Always carry €20-50 in cash.

culturalTips: Tipping in restaurants: Round up the bill or add 5-10% directly when paying the server (do not leave coins on the table).
Traditional Viennese coffeehouse culture encourages lingering for hours with a newspaper without being rushed.
Sundays are quiet days ('Ruhetag'); nearly all supermarkets, shops, and pharmacies are closed.
Punctuality and formal titles (Herr/Frau) are valued in professional and service interactions.

name: Budapest
description: Thermal baths, ruin bars and grand riverside architecture at a low price.
languages: English (spoken in central Budapest and hotels)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cards and phone taps are standard across Budapest. Small cash in Forints is useful for thermal bath lockers and market hall vendors.

culturalTips: Tradition states Hungarians do not clink beer glasses when toasting (historically related to the 1848 revolution defeat), though it is relaxing among youth.
Check the restaurant receipt for 'szervizdíj' (service charge, usually 10-15%); if included, no additional tip is needed.
Thermal baths (Széchenyi, Gellért) require swimming caps in lap pools and flip-flops on wet tiles.
Validate transit tickets before boarding the Budapest metro; ticket inspectors check frequently and issue instant fines.

name: Athens
description: The Acropolis, lively food scene and ancient sites close to modern neighborhoods.
languages: English (very widely spoken across islands and hospitality)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Card machines are legally required in Greece, but smaller island tavernas, beach sunbed rentals, and ferries strongly appreciate or request cash.

culturalTips: Tipping: Leaving 5-10% in cash for taverna waitstaff is customary and greatly appreciated.
Do NOT flush toilet paper down the toilet in Greece (including Greek islands)—plumbing pipes are narrow; use the provided lidded wastebin.
Meals are relaxed and late: lunch is 2:00-4:00 PM, dinner is 9:00 PM or later.
The open palm gesture facing someone ('moutza') with fingers spread is an offensive insult in Greek culture.

name: Santorini
description: Clifftop villages with sunset views over a volcanic caldera. Very crowded in peak summer.
languages: English (very widely spoken across islands and hospitality)

name: Dubrovnik
description: Walled medieval city on the Adriatic with island day trips.
languages: English (widely spoken along the Adriatic coast & Zagreb)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cards are widely accepted, but cash in Euros is needed for island water taxis, beach rentals, small bakeries, and farmers markets.

culturalTips: Croatia's coffee culture ('idemo na kavu') is about leisurely sitting for hours in outdoor cafes talking with friends.
Tipping: 10% in restaurants for good service is standard, usually given in cash.
Modest dress is required when entering historic churches and cathedrals (cover shoulders and knees).
Tap water is remarkably clean and delicious throughout Croatia.

description: Adriatic islands, national parks with waterfalls and walled coastal towns.
languages: English (widely spoken along the Adriatic coast & Zagreb)

name: Istanbul
description: Mosques, bazaars and ferry rides across two continents.
languages: English (spoken in Istanbul tourist zones and coastal resorts)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Credit card and contactless acceptance is high across Istanbul and tourist cities. Keep Turkish Lira notes for yellow taxis, street simit carts, and tips.

culturalTips: Tipping: Leaving 10% in sit-down restaurants is customary and appreciated; round up taxi fares to the nearest convenient note.
Remove your shoes before entering any mosque (shoes are carried in plastic bags provided at the door); women must cover their hair with a scarf.
Turkish hospitality: Accepting offered small tulip glasses of black tea ('çay') or Turkish coffee is polite and builds warm rapport with merchants.
Pick up an Istanbulkart for public transit (metro, ferries, trams) right outside the airport or stations.

name: Reykjavik
description: Small capital and base for geothermal pools, waterfalls and northern lights trips.
languages: English (spoken fluently by virtually the entire population)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: 100% cashless country. You will literally never need physical currency in Iceland; cards and phone taps are accepted everywhere, even pay-toilets in national parks.

culturalTips: Tipping is NOT part of Icelandic culture and is never expected (all service charges, living wages, and taxes are built in).
Thermal pool shower etiquette is strictly enforced: you must shower naked with soap in gender-segregated showers BEFORE putting on your swimsuit and entering geothermal pools.
Never drive off-road: Arctic tundra takes decades to recover from tire tracks, and off-road driving carries severe legal fines.
Tap water everywhere in Iceland is pure untreated glacial spring water—never buy bottled water.

description: Lake towns beneath huge peaks with trains, hiking and skiing.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Card acceptance is widespread, but small Swiss Franc notes/coins are useful for mountain cable cars, honesty farm stands, and public restrooms.

culturalTips: Tipping is included by Swiss law; rounding up to the nearest franc or adding 5% for exceptional service is normal.
Quiet hours ('Ruhezeit') from 10:00 PM to 7:00 AM and all day Sunday are taken very seriously.
Public transport runs with absolute clockwork precision; trains leave the exact second scheduled.
Tap water from public fountains is pristine and safe to drink unless marked 'Kein Trinkwasser'.

name: Marrakech
description: Souks, riads and spice-filled food stalls, with desert and mountain trips nearby.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Morocco is heavily cash-based. Credit cards work in upscale restaurants and riads, but souks, taxis, street food, and tips strictly require physical Dirhams.

culturalTips: Haggling is an expected, social sport in the medinas—negotiate with polite smiles and tea.
Dress conservatively in public and medina streets (cover shoulders, cleavage, and knees).
Always ask permission and agree on a small tip before taking photos of people or snake charmers in Jemaa el-Fnaa.
Tipping 10% in restaurants and giving small coins to bathroom attendants or luggage porters is customary.

name: Cairo
description: The pyramids of Giza and a massive museum scene in a busy, intense city.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash is essential. Credit cards work at major archaeological sites and hotels, but taxis, felucca rides, tips, and bazaars require Egyptian pounds in small bills.

culturalTips: 'Baksheesh' (tipping/gratuity) is an integral cultural expectation for almost every small service (restroom attendants, drivers, luggage, temple guardians).
Dress conservatively: cover shoulders, chest, and knees when walking around public streets and mosques.
Always use your right hand when shaking hands, eating, or giving money.
Lively haggling is customary in markets (souks)—start by offering roughly half the initial asking price with good humor.

name: Cape Town
description: Table Mountain, penguins, vineyards and coastal drives. Use standard city safety precautions.
languages: 11 official languages including English, Zulu, Xhosa, and Afrikaans

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Card and phone tap acceptance is exceptionally high across South Africa. Keep small Rand notes for informal car guards ('parking attendants') and petrol station attendants.

culturalTips: Tipping: 10-15% in sit-down restaurants is customary and expected. Tipping R5-10 to informal parking attendants and petrol station attendants who pump fuel is standard.
Be security-conscious: do not leave bags or phones visible on car seats ('smash-and-grab' prevention), and avoid walking alone after dark in city centers.
'Now' means eventually; 'Just now' means in a little while; 'Now now' means immediately.
Tap water in urban South Africa (Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban) is among the cleanest and safest to drink in the world.

name: Serengeti
description: Safari plains famous for the wildebeest migration.
languages: English (official, widely used in higher education & safari tourism)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: U.S. Dollars (crisp, post-2013 bills) are accepted for safari park fees, international hotels, and hot air balloon rides. Tanzanian Shillings in cash are needed for local markets, food, and tipping.

culturalTips: Tipping on safari is customary: budget $15-20/day for your driver-guide and $10-15/day for camp staff.
In Zanzibar (predominantly Muslim), dress modestly outside beach resorts—cover shoulders and knees in Stone Town and villages.
Always greet people with warmth ('Jambo' or 'Habari') before asking questions or starting transactions.
Single-use plastic bags are strictly prohibited by Tanzanian environmental law.

name: Petra
description: Rock-carved ancient city reached on foot, with desert landscapes at Wadi Rum nearby.
languages: English (widely spoken in tourist destinations like Petra, Amman, Wadi Rum)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash in JOD is required for Bedouin camps in Wadi Rum, camel/donkey handlers in Petra, taxis, and small souvenir stands. Cards work in upscale Amman restaurants and hotels.

culturalTips: Hospitality is an ancient Bedouin point of pride: accepting offered cardamom tea or Arabic coffee is polite (wiggle your small cup side-to-side when finished to signal you're done).
Dress modestly in towns, holy sites, and religious areas (cover shoulders, chest, and knees).
Tipping ('baksheesh') of 10% is customary for drivers, guides, and restaurant staff.
Always use your right hand when eating, greeting, and exchanging money.

name: Dubai
description: Skyscrapers, malls, desert tours and beaches. Very hot in summer.

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Almost entirely cashless. Cards and phone taps work everywhere from taxis to malls; cash is only needed for small souk stalls and tips.

culturalTips: Dress modestly in public places (shoulders and knees covered outside beach resorts).
Public displays of affection beyond holding hands are culturally frowned upon and can lead to fines.
Tipping 10-15% in restaurants is standard and appreciated for hospitality staff.
During Ramadan, eating, drinking, or chewing gum in public during daylight hours is restricted.

name: Tokyo
description: Giant, safe, efficient city with extraordinary food at every price point.
languages: English (basic signage in major train stations, limited spoken fluency outside hotels)

cardsLimited: Discover (accepted where JCB is accepted via network partnership)
paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash remains important! While digital pay has expanded rapidly, ramen ticket vending machines, historic temples/shrines, coin lockers, and small izakayas are still CASH ONLY.
paymentMethods.transitTip: Suica / Pasmo IC Card: Add a digital Suica or Pasmo to your Apple Wallet / Google Wallet before landing to tap seamlessly across all Tokyo trains, subways, and convenience stores.

culturalTips: NO TIPPING under any circumstances—tipping in Japan is considered confusing, awkward, or even rude; great service is standard.
Eat or drink on the spot; walking while eating or drinking street food is considered bad manners.
Keep public voice levels very low on subway and commuter trains; phone calls on trains are strictly forbidden.
Public trash cans are almost nonexistent in cities: be prepared to carry your trash in your bag until you return to your hotel or find a convenience store bin.

name: Seoul
description: Palaces, markets, Korean barbecue and late-night energy.
languages: English (subway signage in English, varying spoken fluency)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Virtually 100% card-friendly. However, you MUST buy and reload a physical T-Money transit card with CASH at convenience stores or subway kiosks.
paymentMethods.transitTip: T-Money Card: Buy a T-Money card at any convenience store and reload with CASH to tap on subways, buses, and taxis.

culturalTips: NO TIPPING in South Korea—service charges are included, and tips are not expected.
Use two hands (or place your left hand supporting your right forearm) when handing or receiving drinks, money, or business cards to show respect.
Pour drinks for your companions, never for yourself; let others refill your cup when empty.
Download Naver Map or KakaoMap: Google Maps does not provide walking/driving directions in South Korea due to national security data laws.

name: Taipei
description: Night markets, hot springs and mountain trails within the metro area.

popularEWallets: EasyCard / iPASS (essential transit & convenience store card)
paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash is essential for famous night markets, street food stalls, and traditional breakfast spots. An EasyCard is vital for all subways, buses, YouBikes, and convenience stores.

culturalTips: NO TIPPING in Taiwan—restaurant bills include a 10% service charge where applicable; tips are not expected.
Eating, drinking (even water), and chewing gum are strictly prohibited inside MRT subway stations and trains, carrying instant NT$1,500 fines.
Stand on the right on MRT escalators to allow people in a rush to pass on the left.
Never stick chopsticks vertically into a bowl of rice (it resembles incense sticks burned for the deceased at funerals).

name: Hong Kong
description: Skyline views, dim sum and surprisingly good hiking right outside the city.
languages: English (official, widely spoken in business & transport)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Octopus card and credit cards dominate, but traditional dim sum tea houses (cha chaan tengs) and red taxis frequently remain CASH ONLY.
paymentMethods.transitTip: Octopus Card: Pick up an Octopus card at the airport MTR desk or add digital Octopus to Apple Wallet—essential for MTR, Star Ferry, and convenience stores.

culturalTips: Pick up an Octopus card at the airport immediately: it pays for MTR subways, ferries, convenience stores, and vending machines.
At traditional Cantonese dim sum tables, tap two fingers on the table when someone pours your tea as a silent gesture of gratitude.
A 10% service charge is usually added to restaurant bills; rounding up small change is customary.
Hong Kong moves fast: walk briskly and avoid stopping suddenly in the middle of busy pedestrian walkways or MTR tunnels.

name: Bangkok
description: Street food, temples and rooftop bars in a hot, chaotic and affordable city.
languages: English (widely understood in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, and tourist islands)

paymentMethods.cashAdvice: Cash is king in Thailand! While hotels, shopping malls, and upscale dining take credit cards, all street food stalls, tuk-tuks, night markets, and massage parlors require physical Baht.

culturalTips: The 'Wai' greeting: Place your palms together at your chest and bow your head slightly to greet or thank people.
Deep reverence for the Royal Family: Defaming or disrespecting the King or monarchy ('lèse-majesté') is a severe crime punishable by imprisonment.
Remove shoes before stepping into temples, traditional shops, and private homes.
Never touch anyone on top of their head, and never point the soles of your feet at any person, Buddha statue, or royal portrait.

languages: English (widely understood in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, and tourist islands)
